clinicalPearls: Defined as non-functioning lung tissue that lacks normal communication with the tracheobronchial tree and receives an anomalous systemic arterial supply, most often from the descending thoracic or abdominal aorta.

Two subtypes exist: intralobar (shares the visceral pleura of normal lung and typically presents later in childhood or adulthood with recurrent infection) and extralobar (has its own pleural investment, presents earlier and is frequently associated with other anomalies).
Intralobar sequestration predominates and characteristically involves the posterobasal segment of the left lower lobe.
Venous drainage differs by subtype: intralobar lesions usually drain to the pulmonary veins, whereas extralobar lesions typically drain to systemic veins such as the azygos or hemiazygos system.
CT angiography is the investigation of choice because it demonstrates the anomalous systemic feeding vessel that clinches the diagnosis.
Extralobar lesions are commonly detected antenatally and may coexist with congenital diaphragmatic hernia, congenital pulmonary airway malformation (hybrid lesions) and cardiac defects.
Definitive management is surgical resection (lobectomy for intralobar disease, simple excision for extralobar), while catheter embolisation of the feeding artery is an option in selected cases.
Meticulous identification and secure control of the systemic feeding artery is essential, as an unrecognised retracted vessel can cause catastrophic haemorrhage.
reference.pathophysiology: During foetal development an accessory lung bud arises from the primitive foregut caudal to the normal lung bud, and because it develops separately it fails to establish communication with the tracheobronchial tree and retains its embryonic systemic arterial supply from the aorta rather than acquiring a pulmonary arterial connection. Whether the ectopic tissue is incorporated within the developing lung before or after pleural formation determines the intralobar phenotype (no separate pleura) versus the extralobar phenotype (separate pleural investment). The sequestered tissue is non-aerated or ventilated only through collateral channels, predisposing to mucus stasis and recurrent infection, while its systemic arterial supply creates a shunt that can rarely produce high-output cardiac strain or life-threatening haemoptysis.
additionalDifferentials: Posterior mediastinal mass such as neuroblastoma
additionalInvestigations: CT pulmonary and aortic angiography to define the feeding artery and venous drainage
Contrast-enhanced MRI or MR angiography (avoids ionising radiation, useful in children)
Echocardiography to assess shunt burden and exclude associated cardiac anomalies
Digital subtraction angiography if embolisation is planned
Histopathological examination of the resected specimen
Renal and spinal imaging where associated anomalies are suspected in extralobar disease
redFlags: Massive or recurrent haemoptysis from the systemic arterial supply
Signs of high-output cardiac failure in a neonate or infant from a large shunt
Rapidly enlarging antenatal lesion with hydrops or mediastinal shift
Recurrent lower-lobe pneumonia refractory to treatment
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is excellent after complete resection, with low recurrence and preserved long-term pulmonary function. Outcome in antenatally detected disease depends on lesion size, associated anomalies and the presence of hydrops.
pitfalls: Failing to obtain dedicated angiographic imaging and thereby missing the anomalous systemic artery, risking intraoperative haemorrhage.
Mislabelling a hybrid lesion as pure sequestration or pure congenital pulmonary airway malformation.
Overlooking an infradiaphragmatic feeding vessel arising from the abdominal aorta.
Attributing recurrent left basal pneumonia to ordinary infection rather than an underlying sequestration.
Assuming all lesions drain to pulmonary veins and misjudging the venous anatomy at surgery.
references: Fraser and Paré's Diagnosis of Diseases of the Chest
